items.title: 4.1 Work done by a constant force

source_refs.note: Topic 4.1 with the chapter's opening lines and Figs. 4.1 to 4.4 (PDF 75-76, printed 72-73). The learning objectives are not reproduced; the running header reads 'Work, Energy and Force'.

blocks.text: Work is often thought of in terms of physical or mental effort. In physics, however, the term work involves two things: (i) force and (ii) displacement. We begin with the simple situation in which work is done by a constant force.

blocks.title: Work by a constant force
blocks.text: Consider an object pulled by a constant force F which displaces it through a displacement d in the direction of the force. Work W is defined as the product of the magnitude of the force F and the magnitude of the displacement d: W = F d ... (4.1).

Equation 4.1 shows that if the displacement is zero, no work is done even if a large force is applied: pushing on a wall may tire your muscles, but the work done is zero (Fig. 4.1). The force applied on a body may not always be in the direction of the displacement (Fig. 4.2). If the force F makes an angle theta with the displacement d, the work done equals the product of the component of the force along the direction of the displacement and the magnitude of the displacement: W = (F cos theta) d = F d cos theta ... (4.2), or W = F . d ... (4.3) (Fig. 4.3). Equation 4.3 shows that work is a scalar quantity. The unit of work is the joule (J); from Eq. 4.1, 1 J = 1 N m.

blocks.alt: A person leans forward and pushes a wall with both hands; a red arrow shows the force F on the wall. The wall does not move, and a note says d = 0, so W = F d cos theta = 0 however hard the person pushes.
blocks.caption: A person pushing a wall: force but no displacement, so no work (original diagram after Figure 4.1).

blocks.text: When a constant force acts through a distance d, the event can be plotted on a simple graph (Fig. 4.4), the distance along the x-axis and the force along the y-axis. As the force does not vary, the graph is a horizontal straight line. If the constant force F (newton) and the displacement d (metre) are in the same direction, the work done is F d (joule); the shaded area in Fig. 4.4 is also F d, so the area under a force-displacement curve can be taken to represent the work done by the constant force. If the force is not in the direction of the displacement, the graph is plotted between F cos theta and d.

items: If theta is less than 90 degrees, work is done and it is said to be positive work.
If theta = 90 degrees, no work is done.
If theta is greater than 90 degrees, the work done is said to be negative.
The SI unit of work is N m, known as the joule (J).

blocks.long_description: Work is the product of the force component along the displacement and the displacement, so a force at right angles to the motion or a force with no displacement does no work, and a force opposing the motion does negative work; on a force-displacement graph a constant force gives a rectangle whose area is the work. When the force varies, the path is cut into short intervals over which the force is nearly constant, the work in each is the force component times the interval, and in the limit of vanishing intervals the total work is the area under the curve of the force component against displacement. Gravity does the same work minus mgh between two points whatever the path, and zero round a closed path, which makes it a conservative force, unlike friction, whose work grows with the length of the path. Power is the rate of doing work, equal to the force times the velocity, measured in watts, with the kilowatt-hour as the commercial unit of electrical energy.
